title: Limits at Infinity and Orders of Growth
quickIdea: As x grows, only the fastest-growing term matters: logarithms lose to powers, and powers lose to exponentials.
remember: For a ratio of polynomials at infinity, divide numerator and denominator by the highest power present.
Growth ladder: ln x grows slower than any positive power x^p, and x^p grows slower than any exponential e^(a x) with a > 0.
Consequences: lim(x->inf) (ln x)/x = 0, lim(x->inf) x^p/e^(a x) = 0, lim(x->inf) x^(1/x) = 1.
A bounded oscillation is invisible next to x: (x - sin x)/(x + cos x) -> 1 because sin x and cos x are trapped between -1 and 1.
Limits at infinity are one-sided by nature: x -> +infinity and x -> -infinity can give different answers for the same function.
e^(-x) decays so fast that (1 + x^2) e^(-x) -> 0 even though x^2 grows without bound.

example.work: Divide every term by x^3: (3 - 2/x^2 + 1/x^3)/(1 + 5/x^3). Each of 2/x^2, 1/x^3 and 5/x^3 tends to 0, leaving 3/1.
example.answer: The limit is 3 - the ratio of the leading coefficients, which is why the division is the whole method.

gateAngle: 2015 Set 1 Q.4 is the classic: lim(x->inf) x^(1/x) = 1, answered either by taking logs or by the growth ladder. The same ladder decides the trap in that question, where 'anything to the power 0 is 1' gives the right answer for the wrong reason.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Evaluate lim(x->inf) (x - sin x)/(x + cos x).
variations.answer: 1. Divide numerator and denominator by x: (1 - (sin x)/x)/(1 + (cos x)/x), and both sine and cosine quotients tend to 0 because they are bounded.
variations.why: A bounded numerator cannot beat x. This is the squeeze idea, and it is the reason L'Hopital must not be attempted here - the derivative ratio oscillates.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Which is larger for very large x: x^100 or e^x?
variations.answer: e^x, eventually. For every fixed p, x^p/e^x -> 0 as x -> infinity, so the exponential overtakes any power however large the power is.
variations.why: The comparison is asymptotic, not pointwise: at x = 1000, x^100 is enormous, yet e^x is vastly larger still. GATE tests the eventual ordering.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Evaluate lim(x->inf) (1 + x^2) e^(-x).
variations.answer: 0. Rewrite as (1 + x^2)/e^x and divide by x^2: (1/x^2 + 1)/(e^x/x^2), whose denominator tends to infinity while the numerator tends to 1.
variations.why: This is GATE CSE 2015 Set 3 Q.9's shape, and it is the growth ladder applied directly: the exponential in the denominator wins.

trap.what: Assuming a limit at infinity is infinite whenever the expression contains growing terms, or using L'Hopital reflexively on infinity/infinity.
trap.why: What matters is the comparison between numerator and denominator, not their sizes separately. And L'Hopital is valid only when the derivative ratio has a limit, which bounded oscillation defeats.
trap.counterexample: x^(1/x) -> 1 and not infinity, although both base and exponent grow. (x + sin x)/x -> 1 although the derivative ratio (1 + cos x)/1 has no limit.

check.question: Evaluate lim(x->inf) 2^x / x^2.
check.explanation: The exponential beats every power, so the ratio grows without bound. Dividing by x^2 gives 2^x/x^2 unchanged in spirit: the numerator's growth dominates.
